answer: Nobody counted carefully before the British. Ottoman figures are estimates; for 1914 they run from about 690,000 people in all, with Jews put at 60,000 to about 85,000. The British census of 1922 found 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews; the last census, in 1931, found about 1,035,000. By the end of 1946 the UN committee estimated about 1,846,000: 1,203,000 Arabs and 608,000 Jews. About 376,000 Jewish immigrants were recorded from 1920 to 1946, most of the Jewish growth. The British and UN inquiries said the Arab growth was almost entirely births exceeding deaths. A minority view says unrecorded Arab immigration mattered more; the best-known book making that case was heavily criticised. So the land was inhabited, mostly by Arabs, and the Jewish share rose from 11 to about 33 percent.

contested.text: Joan Peters's 1984 book argued that much Arab growth was illegal immigration drawn by Zionist prosperity. Most reviewers rejected it. Yehoshua Porath, an Israeli historian, wrote that most of the growth was natural increase, as the British and UN inquiries had found. Daniel Pipes, who had praised the book, conceded serious faults yet held that no reviewer had refuted its central thesis. The economist Fred Gottheil argues that unrecorded illegal immigration from 1922 to 1931 mattered. Our reading: the large majority of the growth was natural increase; some immigration and movement within the country happened but cannot be measured.

could_not_verify: Two facts have only two reliable sites: the Ottoman-era uncertainty and 1914 estimates (the American Jewish Year Book and the Survey of Palestine are both on bjpa.org, one site), and the end-of-1944 estimate. I found no third readable independent page for them.

The end-of-1946 figures: UNSCOP and the Mandate government's 1947 Supplement to the Survey (reproduced in a 1949 UN paper, whose scan is garbled) are the documents; the Supplement itself was not found online. I found no independent scholar or news page that repeats the Arab and Jewish split.

Ottoman census totals (Karpat, McCarthy) were not read; Justin McCarthy's book is under copyright and I did not cite it. The Journal of Palestine Studies demography article, UN University Press table and a mideastweb.org summary were not readable.
The 1931 census report is an unreadable scan here; its figures come from the Survey, ECF, Emory's quotation and the news item.

The Survey of Palestine and the Anglo-American report give the Jewish and Arab counts but differ in total (1,765,000 vs 1,727,786 in the American Jewish Year Book) because of how they count forces and nomads; I did not resolve it.
UNSCOP's own table of religions gives a 1922 Muslim figure (486,177) that does not match the census (590,890); I cite only its prose paragraphs.
I did not find a readable page by a demographer arguing that Arab growth from 1922 to 1946 was mostly immigration other than Gottheil on 1922-1931.
not_claimed: This card does not say there was no Arab immigration into Palestine, only that the official inquiries put it at a small share of the growth.
It does not say the Jewish population was small in 1947; it says it was about a third.
It does not give the Arab population by origin or say how many Arab families were in their villages for generations.
It does not say the land was 'empty' or 'full': counts alone do not settle that.
